properties.plot_themes_description: Through episodic newsroom stories the series interrogates journalistic ethics, civic responsibility, and social issues such as corruption, inequality, and civil rights.
properties.description: Lou Grant (debut 1977) is an American drama created by James L. Brooks, Allan Burns and Gene Reynolds that shifts a familiar sitcom figure into a hard-hitting newsroom drama. Starring Edward Asner alongside Robert Walden and Mason Adams, the series follows a newspaper city editor and his reporting staff as they investigate crime, corruption, and topical social issues. Across its run the show balanced investigative procedure with character-driven moral dilemmas and earned widespread critical acclaim for its courageous, socially conscious storytelling.

properties.plot_themes_description: The series probes family dynamics and class divisions as two brothers pursue competing visions of success, revealing the costs of ambition and the impact of postwar social and political upheaval.
properties.description: Rich Man, Poor Man (1976) is a television miniseries adaptation of Irwin Shaw's novel that chronicles the lives of the Jordache family from the end of World War II into the 1960s. Directed by David Greene with a score by Alex North, the series features Peter Strauss, Nick Nolte, Susan Blakely, Ed Asner and a large supporting cast. The drama traces two brothers whose opposing choices—one seeking corporate success and the other living recklessly—expose class tensions, family loyalties, and the broader social and political currents of postwar America. Emotionally intense and melodramatic, the series blends intimate character study with sweeping, period-rooted storytelling.

properties.plot_themes_description: The series emphasizes intergenerational family bonds, communal responsibility, religious faith and moral decision-making. Recurrent themes include perseverance through economic and environmental hardship, the responsibilities and limits of neighborliness, coming-of-age and the formation of personal character, and the negotiation between traditional values and changing social circumstances on the frontier.
properties.description: Little House on the Prairie (1974) is an American Western–historical family drama developed for television with Michael Landon serving as a leading creative force (star, producer and frequent director). The principal ensemble includes Michael Landon as the family patriarch, Karen Grassle as his wife, and Melissa Gilbert as their daughter, supported by a recurring town ensemble. Set in the late 19th century on a farm near a small Minnesota town, the series follows the family’s daily work, the children’s schooling and growth, and the community’s responses to hardship, illness and moral dilemmas. Combining Western frontier settings with period-accurate domestic detail, the show foregrounds themes of familial loyalty, faith, communal solidarity and perseverance in the face of adversity. Its emotional aim is comforting and earnest storytelling—heartwarming and occasionally bittersweet—intended to provide moral lessons and nostalgic reflection for a family-oriented audience.

entities.name: The Waltons

properties.plot_themes_description: Explores intergenerational family bonds, coming-of-age growth, faith and community resilience, and the ways economic hardship and war reshape ordinary lives.
properties.description: The Waltons (1972–1981), created by Earl Hamner Jr., is a period television drama that follows a large family in the Blue Ridge Mountains of Virginia during the Great Depression and World War II. The ensemble cast includes Richard Thomas, Ralph Waite, Michael Learned, Jon Walmsley, Mary Beth McDonough, Eric Scott, Judy Norton Taylor, Ellen Corby, Will Geer, Kami Cotler, and David Harper. Told frequently through the vantage of the eldest son, an aspiring writer, the series traces coming-of-age arcs, marriages, births, illness, and loss while centering faith, community, and moral steadiness. Tonally nostalgic and heartfelt, it foregrounds domestic labor, local work, and multigenerational bonds against historical upheaval.

properties.plot_themes_description: Examines the bonds and tensions of family life—parental authority, adolescent identity, marital strains, and the push-and-pull between tradition and independence—through intimate domestic episodes.
properties.description: Family (first aired 1976) is a character-driven American television drama focusing on the Lawrence family of suburban Pasadena. The series stars Sada Thompson, James Broderick and Gary Frank and was notable for its emphasis on everyday domestic conflicts, coming-of-age storylines, and nuanced character work. Produced in the late 1970s with contributions from producers Edward Zwick and Marshall Herskovitz, the show balances warmth and poignancy while exploring themes of parenthood, marriage, and intergenerational tension. Its intimate, performance-forward style earned critical praise and multiple Emmy wins for cast members.

properties.plot_themes_description: Episodes examine how personal desires collide with consequence, using fantastical scenarios to explore redemption, moral choice, and the gap between fantasy and reality.
properties.description: Fantasy Island (first aired 1977) is an episodic, family-oriented fantasy-adventure series starring Ricardo Montalban and Hervé Villechaize, with Wendy Schaal among the recurring cast. The show centers on a mysterious island resort where an enigmatic host fulfills guests' fantasies, which often take unexpected, morally charged turns; episodes blend romance, supernatural elements, and guest-driven stories. Across its run the series emphasized wistful, sometimes melancholy storytelling, focusing on redemption, consequences, and the collision between wish and reality. Its emotional tone mixes nostalgic warmth with eerie suspense and moral reflection.

properties.plot_themes_description: Weekly onboard vignettes explore romantic connections, interpersonal friendships, and the escapist pleasures of brief encounters and second chances.
properties.description: The Love Boat (premiering 1977) is an American comedy-drama built around the romantic and comic tales of passengers and the crew of a cruise ship. The series starred an ensemble including Gavin MacLeod, Bernie Kopell, Ted Lange, Fred Grandy, Lauren Tewes, Jill Whelan, and later Ted McGinley, and ran for multiple seasons with hundreds of episodes. Each installment weaves several self-contained guest-star stories alongside recurring shipboard characters, blending light comedy, romance, and sentimental moments. The show trades on escapism, nostalgia, and upbeat resolutions to offer broad family-friendly entertainment.

entities.name: Centennial

properties.plot_themes_description: The narrative examines settlement and westward expansion, changing relationships between peoples and the land, cultural clashes, and the moral and generational consequences of progress.
properties.description: Centennial is a 1978 American 12-episode television miniseries adapted from James A. Michener's novel that chronicles roughly two centuries of Colorado history. The production assembles a large ensemble cast and follows multiple families as settlement, industry, and cultural conflict reshape the region. Combining epic scope with intimate, character-driven scenes, the series explores themes of legacy, identity, and the human relationship to the land, delivered in a nostalgic yet often somber tone.

properties.plot_themes_description: The series explores class conflict and social mobility in a coastal community through intertwined stories of romantic rivalry, economic struggle, family duty and personal resilience.
properties.description: Poldark (first broadcast in the 1970s) is a televised adaptation of Winston Graham's historical novels starring Robin Ellis, Angharad Rees and Clive Francis that blends drama, romance and historical detail. Set in late-18th-century Cornwall, it follows a returning veteran who confronts ruined estates, failing mines and fraught romantic entanglements while clashing with an ambitious banking family. The production is notable for extensive location shooting, faithful period costuming and a restrained score that together create an evocative, character-driven period piece. The series examines class tensions, economic hardship and personal loyalty with a melancholic, closely observed tone.

properties.plot_themes_description: Through classroom stories and faculty interactions, the series explores tolerance, race and class dynamics, institutional constraints, youth identity, and pressing social issues of its era.
properties.description: Room 222 is an American comedy-drama series that premiered in 1969, starring Lloyd Haynes, Denise Nicholas and Michael Constantine, with Karen Valentine in a key supporting role. Set at a large, multicultural Los Angeles high school, the show follows an idealistic history teacher who, with the help of a school counselor and a student teacher, addresses contemporary social issues in character-driven episodes. Praised as groundbreaking and Emmy-recognized, the series blends humor and drama to explore race relations, youth culture, institutional challenges, and tolerance with an earnest, reflective tone.

properties.plot_themes_description: The series uses soap-opera conventions and surreal incidents to explore suburban domesticity, gendered expectations, identity, and the emotional strains of everyday life under social pressures.
properties.description: Mary Hartman, Mary Hartman (1976) is a satirical comedy-drama created in the Norman Lear orbit that stars Louise Lasser alongside Greg Mullavey and Mary Kay Place. Presented without a laugh track, the series parodies soap-opera conventions by following a small-town housewife as increasingly strange, melodramatic, and sometimes violent events unfold around her. Written and shaped by writers such as Gail Parent and Ann Marcus and produced in the mid-1970s, the show blends absurdist humor, social satire, and character-focused drama to examine suburban domestic life and gendered expectations with a darkly comic tone.

properties.plot_themes_description: Focuses on family bonds and parenting while exploring grief, adolescent coming-of-age arcs, sibling dynamics, and the process of rebuilding life after loss.
properties.description: Eight Is Enough (1977–1981) is a family comedy-drama starring Dick Van Patten with early appearances by Lani O'Grady and Connie Needham and later additions including Betty Buckley and Grant Goodeve. The series follows a father raising eight children as the household navigates adolescence, sibling tensions, the death of the mother, and eventual remarriage, blending humor with earnest emotional moments. Its storytelling centers on domestic life, parenting dilemmas, and the family's process of grieving and adaptation. The tone is warm and sentimental, aiming for relatable, character-driven episodes that mix light comedy with heartfelt drama.

entities.name: Taxi

properties.plot_themes_description: The show examines the bonds between coworkers as they confront economic precarity, personal ambitions, and emotional isolation while trying to reconcile dreams with everyday urban life.
properties.description: Taxi (1978–1983) is an American ensemble sitcom that follows the drivers and dispatcher of a New York City taxicab company as they cope with work, friendship, and personal ambitions. The series features strong performances from Judd Hirsch, Jeff Conaway, Danny DeVito and a supporting ensemble including Marilu Henner, Tony Danza, Christopher Lloyd, Andy Kaufman, Rhea Perlman, Randall Carver, and Carol Kane. Combining broad situational comedy with quieter, poignant episodes, the show explores themes of aspiration, working-class struggle, identity, and found-family bonds while maintaining a warm yet bittersweet emotional tone.

properties.plot_themes_description: Examines how wealth and power corrode family bonds and fuel cycles of betrayal, ambition-driven conflicts, revenge, and institutional corruption.
properties.description: Dallas (originally released 1978) is an American prime-time soap opera and drama centered on the wealthy Ewing family and their Texas oil empire. The series, known for its cliffhanger-driven serialized storytelling and melodramatic tone, stars Larry Hagman, Ken Kercheval and Patrick Duffy among a large ensemble cast. Plotlines revolve around power struggles, betrayal, romantic entanglements, and corruption within and between families, often resolved through manipulation, blackmail and revenge. The show blends glossy, glamorous visuals with tense, suspenseful storytelling and a strongly emotive, addictive tone.

properties.plot_themes_description: The work examines how severe childhood abuse fractures identity and memory, the ethical and emotional complexities of psychotherapy, and the difficult, incremental path toward integration and healing.
properties.description: Sybil (1976), directed by Daniel Petrie and starring Sally Field, Joanne Woodward and Brad Davis, is a biographical drama telefilm adapted from Flora Rheta Schreiber's book. The story follows a young woman who, after enduring severe childhood abuse, manifests multiple distinct personalities and enters an intensive therapeutic relationship with a devoted psychiatrist. The film is a psychological, character-driven study of trauma, memory and identity, notable for its emotional intensity, intimate direction and award-winning central performances. Its tone is harrowing yet compassionate, exploring both the ethical complications and the healing possibilities of psychotherapy.

properties.plot_themes_description: Examines the nature of artistic performance, cultural tradition, emotional expression, and the collaborative process of staging and interpreting works across genres.
properties.description: Great Performances is a long-running American television anthology that presents filmed versions of stage works for a national audience. The series showcases plays, musicals, operas, ballets and concert programs featuring performers such as Julie Andrews, Plácido Domingo and conductor Scott Yoo. Episodes vary from intimate dramatic pieces to large-scale musical spectacles, highlighting choreography, orchestral performance and production design across diverse cultural traditions. Typically produced in color and rated TV‑G, the series brings theatrical and classical performance into the television format.

entities.name: The Rockford Files

properties.plot_themes_description: Stories center on a search for personal redemption and rough‑edged justice, exploring loyalty and family ties amid moral ambiguity and local corruption.
properties.description: The Rockford Files (1974) is an American crime-drama series created by Roy Huggins and Stephen Cannell, starring James Garner as a laconic ex-con who works as a private investigator. Set in Malibu and often filmed with a down-to-earth, sunlit look, the show follows the detective as he runs a modest-fee practice from a beachside trailer and navigates cases that mix petty scams with larger conspiracies. Supporting players such as Noah Beery Jr. and Joe Santos populate a cast of eccentric allies and shady associates, while recurring themes include redemption, loyalty, and moral ambiguity. The result is a character-driven procedural that blends tense investigations with dry humor and an empathetic, world-weary lead.

properties.plot_themes_description: The series probes class and power by repeatedly placing a working-class, unpretentious investigator against wealthy, socially privileged suspects who underestimate him. Themes of justice and moral inevitability recur, emphasizing persistence, methodical reasoning, and the gap between appearance and truth. The stories examine perception versus reality—how polished façades conceal motive and how small, overlooked details reveal culpability.
properties.description: Columbo is a landmark television crime drama that launched as a regular series in 1971, created by Richard Levinson and William Link and starring Peter Falk as a rumpled but brilliant Los Angeles lieutenant. Presented largely as an inverted detective format, episodes typically reveal the crime and perpetrator up front and then follow the lieutenants genial, probing method as he teases out contradictions and small physical clues. The series emphasizes psychological maneuvering, moral contrast between social classes, and character performance over action spectacle; its tone mixes wry humor, patience, and moral clarity. Produced for the NBC Mystery Movie wheel and later revived in subsequent decades, the show is celebrated for Falks iconic portrayal, the recurring just one more thing device, and a parade of high-profile guest stars.

properties.plot_themes_description: Through soap-opera parody and serialized storytelling, the series explores family dysfunction, sexual and gender identity, infidelity, crime, addiction, and religious and social taboos while satirizing class and cultural norms.
properties.description: Soap is a 1977 primetime American sitcom that parodies daytime melodramas by following two interlinked families, the Tates and the Campbells, through serialized, often outrageous storylines. Created and written by Susan Harris, the show featured a large ensemble cast including Katherine Helmond, Cathryn Damon, Richard Mulligan, Robert Guillaume, Billy Crystal, Diana Canova, Jennifer Salt, Robert Mandan and others. Combining satirical comedy and melodrama, it tackled controversial subjects of the era—infidelity, murder, religion, mental illness, sexuality and the mob—while mixing broad farce with unexpectedly affecting dramatic moments. Its provocative tone and serialized structure generated both cultural controversy and critical acclaim, and it launched at least one successful spin-off.

properties.plot_themes_description: The narrative explores cross-cultural encounter and personal identity amid fierce power struggles, competing religious influences, and strict codes of honor.
properties.description: Shogun (1980), directed by Jerry London and adapted from James Clavell's novel, is a multi-part television miniseries starring Richard Chamberlain, Toshirô Mifune and Yôko Shimada. Presented as a historical adventure drama, it follows an English sailor stranded in 17th-century Japan who becomes enmeshed in samurai society and fractious political maneuvering, with competing religious and cultural forces shaping events. The production is notable for its expansive period sets, bilingual storytelling, and emphasis on character-driven intrigue. Viewers praise its immersive tone, complex themes of honor and identity, and its sweeping, epic scale.

properties.plot_themes_description: The series explores female camaraderie and empowerment as women undertake undercover investigations to solve crimes and uphold justice.
properties.description: Charlie's Angels is a 1976 American crime drama series that stars Farrah Fawcett, Kate Jackson and Jaclyn Smith and mixes action, mystery and adventure in weekly self-contained cases. The premise centers on an unseen wealthy employer who assigns investigations by speakerphone to a private detective agency staffed by three former policewomen. Across its episodes the show foregrounds stylish undercover work, ensemble dynamics and light suspense, with themes of female solidarity and empowerment. The tone is often campy and nostalgic, prioritizing glamour and entertainment over gritty realism.

properties.plot_themes_description: The series explores the bond between two partners as they pursue justice amid urban crime, corruption, and the personal costs of police work.
properties.description: Starsky and Hutch is a 1975 American action-crime drama starring Paul Michael Glaser and David Soul, with Antonio Fargas in a supporting role. The series follows two streetwise detectives who chase criminals across San Francisco from their signature red-and-white Ford Gran Torino, blending chase-driven action with character-focused buddy dynamics. Episodes range from gritty, drug- and street-crime investigations to lighter, camaraderie-led adventures, and the show emphasizes themes of loyalty, justice, and partnership. Its tone balances high-energy thrills with warm humor and period-specific atmosphere.

entities.name: Happy Days

properties.plot_themes_description: Explores family dynamics, adolescent growth, friendship bonds, and mentorship within a nostalgic portrayal of 1950s American life.
properties.description: Happy Days (1974–1984) is a televised family comedy set in a stylized 1950s Midwestern America, starring Ron Howard, Henry Winkler, Marion Ross, Tom Bosley, and Erin Moran. The series follows a middle-class family and their teenage son as they navigate school, friendships, and everyday moral lessons, often guided by a charismatic greaser who becomes a family mentor. Combining sitcom humor, musical touches, and period detail, the show foregrounds themes of family, coming-of-age, and nostalgia while maintaining a warm, upbeat emotional tone.

properties.plot_themes_description: The show explores the friction between classes, the impact of historic events on private lives, shifting gender expectations, duty versus desire, and the endurance of interpersonal loyalties amid social transformation.
properties.description: Upstairs, Downstairs (original run 1971–1975) is a British period drama created by Jean Marsh and Eileen Atkins that chronicles the lives of the Bellamy family and their servants at 165 Eaton Place. Starring Gordon Jackson, David Langton and Jean Marsh among an ensemble cast, the series blends detailed historical research with character-driven storytelling to depict class tensions, personal loyalties and the impact of major events such as World War I on private lives. Praised for its emotional depth, accuracy of period detail and shifting perspectives between upstairs and downstairs, the show foregrounds themes of duty, social change and moral complexity.

properties.plot_themes_description: Through self-contained investigations the series explores crime, justice and corruption in an urban setting while probing duty, moral ambiguity, and the human cost of policing.
properties.description: Kojak (1973) is an American police drama starring Telly Savalas alongside Dan Frazer and Kevin Dobson, presented in color and rated TV‑PG. The series follows a bald, lollipop‑sucking NYPD detective as he investigates street-level crime in gritty 1970s New York through largely self-contained, procedural episodes. Combining action, mystery and drama, the show emphasizes realistic on-location photography, brisk plotting and morally complex cases that examine corruption, duty and urban decay. Its emotional tone is tense and gritty but anchored by a charismatic, principled lead and a strong ensemble.
